body: A man is at the kitchen table at half past eleven with a laptop and a cup of tea he has let go cold. His wife’s mother has been living with them since the spring. She has almost no English, she does not go out much any more, and she sits in the front room most of the day with the television on mute. He is trying to find her worship music in Turkish. He has been at it forty minutes. He finds a handful of recordings, mostly a choir in a hall with the microphone too far back, and one album that will not play outside the country it came from. He closes the laptop, goes up to bed, and does not mention it in the morning.

There was nothing wrong with his search. He was not looking for anything obscure. He wanted, for a woman in his front room, what any English-speaking believer can have in four seconds without thinking, and it was not there to be had.

The songs on this band were generated. The hosts are synthesised voices. The station art was made by a model. None of that is buried in a footnote, because a ministry that will not be straight about how it works has already given away the thing it came to protect.

That word, generated, is worth slowing down on, because most people hear something in it that is not there. It does not mean nobody was involved. Every song here began with a person deciding what it should say and which passage it should stand on, and ended with a person deciding whether it was fit to go out. What the model did was the middle: the arranging, the voicing, the hundred small craft decisions that used to need a room full of paid professionals and a diary booked six months out. That middle was almost the entire cost of making music, and for a ministry it was the reason most things never got made at all.

The honest case for it is arithmetic. A network of 121 stations, hosted around the clock, with 40 of them broadcasting in 29 languages other than English, carrying original music and artwork for every one, is a project that used to require a staff of hundreds and a budget no small ministry has ever had.

That is why gospel radio has always concentrated in wealthy countries and large languages. Not because the need was there — the need was obviously elsewhere — but because that is where the money was, and a studio hour costs the same whether the song reaches a whole nation or four hundred people. Every ministry that ever wanted to serve a small language hit the same wall, quietly, and told nobody. A tool is judged by what it is pointed at, and the same technology filling the world with noise can be turned to carry the Word into it. AI does not make this work good. It makes it possible.

There is a great deal of fear about these tools and much of it is earned. Everybody has seen what the technology is mostly used for: producing an enormous quantity of things nobody asked for, faster than anyone can read them. It is reasonable to want no part of that. But the argument that the Church should therefore stand back and let this generation of technology be shaped entirely by people with no interest in the Kingdom is not caution. It is surrender, and it was offered about printing, about broadcasting and about the internet, each time by serious people who meant well.

The dial is arranged so the international frequencies sit together in their own stretch of the band, and each is hosted in its own language rather than translated into it afterwards. That distinction is the point. A translated station is something made for somebody else and passed on. A hosted one has its own repertoire, its own idiom and its own hour, because the church in that language has its own way of singing and never needed ours.
Which brings the argument to the part people actually object to. Not the economics. The authorship.

Take the objection at its strongest, because the strong version deserves better than a slogan. A song is supposed to come out of a life. When somebody sings that they have known God to be faithful, part of what makes the line land is the claim behind it — that a real person found it to be true and paid something to find out. A generated song has no such life behind it. That is a genuine loss and should not be waved away, because much of what music does for people is exactly this: it lets you borrow somebody else’s testimony until you have one of your own.
But a song is not the only thing in the room. There is also the person listening.

A woman of forty-one is mopping a corridor on the fourth floor of a hospital at twenty past three in the morning. She has been in the country eleven years. Her children are on the other side of the world where it is already late afternoon, and she has one earphone in because the other ear has to stay on the ward. What is playing is Tagalog. Not an English worship song with a Tagalog version laid over it, but the thing itself, sung the way it is sung at home, with the ornament on the third line that only means anything if you grew up hearing it. She keeps mopping to the end of the corridor. She plays it again the next night, and the night after.

Nobody in that corridor was thinking about how the music was made. The question at twenty past three was whether there was anything in her own language to put in her ear, and for most of eleven years the answer had been not much.

So here is the cost, plainly. Something is genuinely missing from a catalogue made this way. There is no artist whose testimony you can look up, no life that paid for the line, nobody to write to. If what moves you about a hymn is knowing the man wrote it after losing his children at sea, that is not available here and no amount of production will supply it. Anybody who tells you this is the same as the other thing is selling something.

But the comparison is not with the great hymns. It is with silence. The woman in that corridor was not choosing between a generated song in Tagalog and a hymn written out of somebody’s grief in Tagalog. She was choosing between a generated song and nothing, and had been for eleven years. And the life the song came out of is not absent — it is simply not the singer’s. It is the life in the passage the song stands on, paid for by people who did lose everything, and a good deal older than the recording industry.

So the position is narrow enough to hold. The model is a printing press, and a printing press has never once been the author of what it prints. It does not decide what is true. Every station has a remit set by people, every song stands on a passage of Scripture chosen by people, and nothing reaches the air that is not in a catalogue a person approved. What the technology changed is not the message and not the authority. It changed the price of going, and the commission was to go into all the world.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it is worth knowing they are there. There is music, which is most of the band — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards. It is the last of those where the arithmetic in this article stops being an argument.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 328.20 — Türkiye Inspire. It is Turkish-language worship for a church that is very small and very old, in a place a great deal of the New Testament was addressed to. It is also a station no commercial calculation would have produced. There is no business case for it and there never was, which is exactly why the man at the kitchen table found what he found. Put it on for ten minutes even if you have not a word of the language, because this argument is easier to hear than to read: it exists, it did not exist, and what changed was the cost.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a defence. You are entitled to your reservations and may keep every one of them. But go and find the frequency in the language your neighbour speaks, or your mother-in-law, or the woman who cleans the ward you were on, and send it to them this afternoon. Then judge the tool by what it was pointed at, which is the only way anybody has ever sensibly judged a tool.
